They analyze grids of simulated black hole mergers where the collision involves one (or both) of the binary black holes starting out as almost completely flat. The analysis reveals that certain aspects of the gravitational waves emitted, particularly specific frequencies, contain less information about the original state due to the inherent loss of information in these frequencies. Conversely, other aspects of the gravitational waves emitted contain less information about the original state when the associated frequencies do not reach the maximum or minimum possible frequencies. Ultimately, this research suggests that any information about the original state contained in the gravitational waves emitted during the final collapse is constrained by specific mathematical formulas that take into account the shape of the black holes prior to collision. Interestingly, this constraint is more pronounced when the information is contained in the higher frequency aspects of the gravitational waves. Furthermore, this research indicates that any information about the original state contained in the gravitational waves emitted in the lower frequency range is less constrained and can be described by specific mathematical formulas that account for the shape of the black holes prior to collision, leading to a greater range of possibilities in this frequency range. Compared to existing evaluation metrics that only consider one image, we propose a metric that can assess a model's versatility in generating diverse synthetic images.  This novel metric expands upon the traditional precision-recall curve, incorporating a range of metrics, including diversity of pre-trained features, image properties, and learning algorithms.  This curve can be calculated for individual images, sets of images, or even compared to a benchmark using retrieved samples.  In addition to evaluating a model's performance, we utilized this metric to identify areas where a particular model falls short.  Notably, this evaluation metric does not require a domain-matching label, making it more practical and accessible.  We verified the effectiveness of this evaluation metric through comparative testing of a variety of synthesis methods, including classical, generative, and hybrid techniques.  Ultimately, this evaluation metric contributes to the advancement of existing image synthesis methods by pinpointing and addressing their shortcomings.  In turn, this methodology can be applied to various different image synthesis tasks, such as unseen categories and video synthesis.  To support the replication of our results, we made available the implementation and additional evaluation metric visualizations on our website at $\url{https://synthesis-evaluation.github.io/}$.  This site additionally features a range of benchmark curves and pre-trained features for use in future image synthesis benchmarking studies. A comparison with traditional models shows that end-to-end models achieve better results when trained with large amounts of data. Nevertheless, they underperform in scenarios with limited training data. To address this issue, we propose transferring knowledge from similar tasks with the help of a speech synthesizer. This approach enables the model to generate new training data based on unlabelled speech and corresponding transcripts. Finally, we demonstrate that a part of the learned knowledge can be stored in the synthesizer, allowing for further improvements in task performance through fine-tuning of the synthesizer. This knowledge transfer can also be applied to other task architectures and enables the integration of speech synthesis and recognition into a unified system that allows learning and improvement in an end-to-end manner. Overall, our findings reveal the potential of our method for tackling data-related challenges in natural language processing and speech processing. To further explore this potential, we introduce Baseline, an open-source framework that enables the implementation of our proposed knowledge transfer method on a wide range of applications. This tool is designed to facilitate the validation of various types of knowledge transfer between different tasks. To this end, it offers a number of features, including the ability to automatically generate new data, to control the impact of the target task on the source task, and to assess the extent to which the target task influences the source task. Additionally, it features a graph-based representation that facilitates the storage of learned knowledge and allows for the automatic retrieval of that knowledge. academic publishing is a persistent challenge for researchers. A recommender system addressing this issue has gained traction among researchers. Typically, these systems rely on extensive data and compute powerful features. In this paper, we present an alternative approach that uses minimal information about a researcher's writing history to recommend co-authors. Specifically, we propose a method that selects co-authors from a set of general users. Although our focus is on the CS domain, the method can be applied to other fields. We simulate a scenario where we have access to basic information about a researcher's publications and seek to recommend five co-authors for a new paper. We consider two evaluation metrics: Average Preferences and Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain. We developed a dataset with 329K samples based on the Computer Science publications in the past decade. We examined the performance of diverse recommender systems - User-based Similarity Recommendation, Item-based Similarity Recommendation, and several neural network models - and found that User-based Similarity Recommendation performs slightly better than the best neural network model. However, the gap in performance closes significantly when we consider the practical implications of recommending co-authors. To address this limitation, we developed an item-based similarity recommendation system with a more efficient user similarity metric that uses minimal information about a researcher's writing history to recommend co-authors, outperforming the existing state-of-the-art approaches. Furthermore, we found that an item-based similarity recommendation system with a more efficient user similarity metric exhibits similar or better performance in recommending co-authors compared to the standard method. Additionally, we found that recommending co-authors with a more efficient user similarity metric results in significantly fewer impractical recommendations compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods. We discovered that incorporating additional information about researcher entities would enhance the recommending co-authors capabilities. Finally, we found that incorporating researcher profiles would improve recommendation quality but would require more extensive information about each researcher's publication history.   Methods: Carry out the calculation of the elastic scattering of left-right polarized photons with very low energy using the computational tool _nxtool_, which simulates the process with the _JLab_ reactor's deuterium target, considering various final states and different orientations of the photon beam.

  Results: Obtain the dependence of the photon-deuterium elastic scattering cross-section on the initial photon polarization orientation at very low energy, along with its transformation components and photon energy.

  Discussion: Explain the influence of the photon energy and orientation on the elasticity of the photon-deuterium scattering, and demonstrate that at very low energy the concept of elasticity is linked with the coherence of the neutron and proton waves.

  Conclusion: Conclude that at very low energy the elasticity of the photon-deuterium scattering depends on the relative coherence of the neutron and proton waves, which in turn depends on the energy and initial orientation of the photon beam. This leads to the idea that it's possible to reflect the structure of the neutron and proton waves using polarized photodisintegration of the deuterium nucleus at very low energy range.

of non-Hermitian eigenvalue problems that takes advantage of the properties of eigenvalues and eigenvectors in the presence of conditioning.  The method is of a QZ type, leveraging Francis' rotation approach, but modifies it using a separate approach for Givens rotations. This allows for efficient handling of block eigenproblems arising from a quasi-bicritical deflation strategy within Newton's method for nonlinear eigenvalue problems.  Initial experiments indicate the approach maintains the stability and convergence properties of the original method. Notably, this implementation avoids the leverage of extremely small and extremely large deflation factors, a common issue with other methods. Further performance gains are expected in future work by adapting this approach for large-scale deflation within the Lanczos method.  A key benefit of the proposed method is its ability to provide reliable and stable estimates of eigenvalues and eigenvectors even in cases of pathological conditioning.  Specifically, this method maintains proximity to the true eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and does so by controlling the growth of the norm of the eigenvector.  A key theorem has been established to support this claim.  In addition to its general applicability, this method is particularly valuable for the evaluation of extreme eigenvalues in cases of extreme conditioning.  In particular, this method allows for the reliable selection of the dominant eigenvalue in cases of both exact and inexact arithmetic.  A number of interesting cases are presented in support of the conclusions.  We also examine the performance of this method in the evaluation of the Zwanzig projection operator.  Finally, we note that while this method does not provide a direct bound on the error, it does control the growth of the norm of the eigenvector.  Consequently, a post-processing stage is required in order to obtain an approximate eigenvector to a desired accuracy.  A number of techniques for achieving this goal are described in detail.  In addition to standard approaches, two iterative methods are proposed.  In particular, a trust-region approach and a nonlinear Landau-Symplectic iteration method are introduced, and are shown to be effective in sampling eigenspaces and obtaining accurate approximations of eigenvectors.  A number of numerical experiments have been performed in support of the conclusions.  These experiments include testing the method in cases of exact and inexact arithmetic, as well as evaluating its performance on a number of benchmark problems that have been established through collaboration with a number of other researchers.  Consequently, these experiments have provided a number of interesting insights and results.

Working in model-free settings can be beneficial when the target graph is large or model development is complicated.  However, there are several graph recommender system challenges that models struggle with, such as handling diverse graph scales, efficiently processing large graphs, and effectively using neighbor information.  To address these issues, we propose the Neighbor Aggregation Recurrent Model, leveraging direct neighbor information to enhance item representation through aggregated data.  By combining RNN-based model architecture with neighbor aggregation, LABR, surpasses current model-free methods in metrics such as Click-Through-Rate and relative gain on public datasets, and outperforms model-based methods on a transfer learning task. While significant progress has been made in this area, summaries generated by current systems often fail to effectively convey the full range of textual information. In an effort to overcome this limitation, we propose a summary representation technique that strives to comprehensively capture summary content while maintaining accurate relationships with the original text. This approach, rooted in set theory, enables quantitative evaluation of summary inclusiveness and fosters a spirit of competition among systems to produce more inclusive summaries. Through numerical analysis, we demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed method and, in comparative tests, reveal that a system grounded in this framework outperforms existing models on both automatic and human assessments. Importantly, our method identifies a variety of text elements that pose challenges to current summary systems and serves as a potential resource for future research in this area. Ultimately, by promoting summaries that are more inclusive of the original text, we aim to reduce the divide between machine and human comprehension. To circumvent this limitation, we've developed a novel approach that leverages specialized knowledge of a domain via expert input to automatically mark up large amounts of unstructured data. This technique employs the framework of topic layering, combining latent topics and non-negative matrix factorization to identify meaningful subtopics and contextual associations within a corpus. A thorough examination of previously published models has revealed a notable absence of proposed methods for evaluating their performance in an objective manner. In response to this observation, we designed and implemented three novel metrics to determine delirium prediction model quality: classificationmodelconfidence, predictedtimemodality, and occurrenceproportion. These new metrics were applied to conventional classification models trained on standardized ICU delirium data containing patient charts annotated by family members and healthcare professionals. Our proposed metrics have shown the potential to effectively evaluate parallel streams of high-dimensional data in real-time. Furthermore, they have demonstrated the capability to differentiate between clinical and feature-based models in a clinically meaningful way. In our experiments, we have discovered that model confidence performs optimally among the three metrics and is particularly suitable for evaluating parallel streams of high-dimensional data. Ultimately, we believe that our proposed metrics will contribute to the advancement of delirium prediction by making it possible to compare the performance of clinical and feature-based models more effectively. Furthermore, we think that this methodology can be applied to detection and diagnosis challenges that involve predicting patient status based on continuous data streams. Lastly, we provide anonymized ICU data and pre-trained models to the research community for further testing and validation. This data is accessible via the public GitHub repository https://github.com/ikosar/delirium_prediction. We hope that this research facilitates future developments in delirium prediction by providing reproducible results and promoting open comparisons between different methods. A graph allows a PMC if and only if it allows an efficient one, which can be found in polynomial time under a different constraint. We investigate the parameters that determine the size of a PMC in a graph and provide a characterization of those that directly influence it. Specifically, we show that the size of a PMC in a graph directly correlates with its treewidth, independent sets, and the existence of certain subgraphs. This treewidth characterization in particular allows PMCs to be efficiently found in polynomial time in graphs with this property. Our findings also extend to weighted graphs. In addition, we identify the parameters that determine the size of a efficient PMC in a graph and find that they include the treewidth, independent sets, the size of a maximum matching, and the existence of certain subgraphs. Notably, we find that the size of both types of PMCs can be determined efficiently for graphs with a specific treewidth property. Our overall analysis indicates the significance of treewidth in determining PMCs in graphs. This significance is further highlighted in the case of unipolar graphs where the treewidth is 2, and we find that determining the size of a PMC here is an NP-hard problem. Our investigation is also extended to include weighted graphs. Finally, we provide a list of open problems related to PMCs in graphs. Our research utilizes a two-dimensional plasma model comprising electron and ion populations, where we consider the impact of field alignment on wave propagation. Our results show that, when a longitudinal field is present, ion-brillouin waves can be modulated by electron-brillouin waves, provided the field is strongly aligned with the plasma. Conversely, in the absence of ion-brillouin waves or when the field is very weakly aligned, we observe electron-acoustic waves emerging. Additionally, applying transverse fields leads to the suppression of ion-brillouin waves and the emergence of electron-acoustic waves, assuming no ion-brillouin waves are present initially. Our investigation explores the parameters governing these interactions and we model two-dimensional dispersion curves to understand and predict these interactions. Our research will contribute to a deeper understanding of wave propagation in complex plasmas, particularly those involving magnetic fields, and may also have implications for observing ion-brillouin waves in such environments.   Since online RL is susceptible to overfitting a dataset, techniques are employed to mitigate overfitting
  and ensure the learned policy can effectively generalize when applied to unknown environments.
  Among these methods, model selection using theoretical measures is a popular choice.
  However, these theoretical measures often fall short in practice as they typically provide upper bounds on performance that greatly exceed actual expectations.
  In this study, early stopping is proposed as a model selection technique that capitalizes on the training process's capacity to uncover a relevant solution without overfitting it.
  We demonstrate that offline RL training's stop-at-step $K$ can be viewed as a regularized maximum likelihood estimator.
  Utilizing this formulation, we examine generalization error, providing a new upper bound that significantly surpasses current standards with improved assumptions concerning the data and value function approximators.
  Notably, this new bound incorporates the influence of random noise during data generation, providing a quantitative characterization of its impact.
  Additionally, our findings relate risk to the minimum risk principle and, for nonlinear function approximators, establish a crucial requirement for achieving optimal performance with a non-condensing policy.
  Finally, we empirically validate the proposed method with tabular environments, matching its performance to methods employing backward RL.
  In contrast, applying early stopping to model-based methods results in a dramatic decrease in sample efficiency. 
  We hypothesize early stopping may be effective for such methods if they involve a more efficient exploration process. 
  Furthermore, we analyze early stopping with offline policy improvement and evaluate its performance with deep function approximators, observing significant reductions in both performance and stability gaps when compared to methods employing backward RL. 
  With proper tuning, early stopping proves resilient to the noise present in our datasets, with its effectiveness being comporable to methods employing theoretical measures. 
  However, for the deep tabular setting, it falls behind theoretical methods in controlling the gradient explosion issue. 
  We attribute this to early stopping's dependence on the training epoch $K$ being chosen implicitly, which is compparable to an explicit regularizer. 
  We propose a method called modulated early stopping, allowing the control of the gradient explosion issue while maintaining the benefits of early stopping.

In this task, we focus on identifying the style from two possible options - humor and neutrality. While previous attempts at style prediction have been limited to single styles, our dataset, dubbed 'ToLaughOrNotToLaugh', presents a more complex scenario with both humor and neutrality styles represented. In total, our dataset comprises 47K samples, collected from four different internet sources: humor pages, a comedy book summary wiki, a Reddit forum, and general Wikipedia articles.   Methods. This paper specifically examines the case for a network of two detectors, focusing on deriving the likelihood for next generation gravitational wave detectors, including the influence of non-vacuum instrumental conditions. An overview of the results is presented along with an exploration of the most critical factors affecting the likelihood under these conditions. An alternative approach for the likelihood in the null phase scenario is also provided. 

  Results. In this study, a mathematical expression representing the likelihood for a two-detector network is developed, taking into account various factors such as the detector locations, the intrinsic and extrinsic properties of the gravitational wave source, and the instrumental conditions. The results reveal that the most significant influences on the likelihood arise from the detector angle to the source, the intrinsic amplitude, and the differential polarization. The likelihood is shown to be minimally affected by the source's polarization state, the mass of the source, and its distance. The results further indicate that the most substantial impact on the likelihood in the null phase arises from the detector separation while the intrinsic and extrinsic amplitudes play relatively minor roles. 

  Conclusion. The likelihood derived in this study provides a crucial foundation for developing and refining analysis techniques that incorporate the instrumental conditions, which is essential for accurately interpreting the data from the LIGO-Virgo detector network and future collaborations. An important aspect to consider in the analysis of the 3G data. This research offers a valuable perspective on the potential and challenges of working with the data from the next generation of gravitational wave detectors. 

  Upcoming papers in this series will explore the implementation of the likelihood in specific analysis contexts, incorporating the influence of non-vacuum instrumental conditions, and discuss the associated difficulties and possible solutions.

By using text-based annotations, tasks that were previously non-accessible to these models, like medical images and drawings, can be re-defined and their performance improved significantly.   Our study is significant not just for OMR but also for other vision-dominated tasks that are gaining attention, such as Image-to-Text, where our method's potential is immense due to its ability to map unknown pixels to descriptive texts. Similarly, in the task of graph-based drawings, our method shows promising results and can be applied with minimal modifications, and in the domain of medical imaging, our method's value lies in its ability to provide precise and accurate descriptions of the diagnosis process, especially in settings where data is scarce. 

  Our method's main shortcoming is its dependence on a fixed set of tokens, which hinders its performance in situations of unknown symbols during both training and inference processes. It reveals that, in the presence of these fluctuations, particle transport can be modulated in accordance with the fluctuations' properties, resulting in reduced or increased transport. This phenomenon is analogous to the mechanism by which electromagnetic waves induce current in conductors. To further illustrate the underlying dynamics, we investigated the transport of particles confined in a micro-channel under time-dependent influences. Our findings indicate the onset of non-steady movement and oscillations in the density of the particles, dependent on the frequency and intensity of the external fluctuations. Moreover, we observed a connection between these oscillations and the phenomenon of "bottleneck effect." Ultimately, we explored the effect of particle interaction on transport, which led to the observation of two distinct regimes: a non-equilibrium state characterized by reduced transport and a stable equilibrium state with normal transport properties. Our research identifies a new type of dynamics, influenced by the interaction between spatial memory and inertia, that can be observed in diluted complex plasma systems. This interaction causes a transition from regular to irregular movement in the density fluctuations, as the amplitude of the external fluctuations increases. This behavior exhibits the same characteristics as the "multi-fractal" phenomenon observed in complex systems, however, the nature of the observed irregular movements is fundamentally different. In our specific case, the irregular movements are caused by the interaction between spatial memory and inertia, resulting in an array of coexisting states with different properties, and complex oscillation patterns. This phenomenon can be observed not only in the context of particle transport, but also in various other systems, such as the interaction between thermal convection in rotating fluids, and the movement of the atmosphere in planetary systems. Our findings also illustrate the possibility of modulating particle transport by changing the characteristics of external influences, and thus demonstrates the potential of using diluted complex plasma systems as natural "laborsatories" to study the underlying dynamics of these systems. We develop and present an innovative training approach for neural networks based on a novel variant of the Stochastic Gradient Descent method. This approach leverages random walk techniques in both the space of model parameters and the parameter configuration space to facilitate efficient exploration. Traditional gradient-based training methods restrict the model to specific parameter configurations, whereas our method allows the model to also explore the surrounding parameter space during training. We evaluate the effectiveness of our method by applying it to two distinct image classification tasks and compare the results to standard gradient-based training methods. Our experiments demonstrate that this novel training approach yields superior performance on both tasks. Furthermore, we find that this method outperforms self-supervised pre-training methods on a task involving partial data. We also investigate the method's reliance on its initial conditions and find that, in some instances, its performance actually deteriorates when exploring the parameter space. We explain these adverse effects and also identify two potential shortcomings of this training method. Initially, it may cause sudden abrupt declines in accuracy. Secondly, it may induce the creation of exotic models that fail to achieve comparable results when testing them with different data. Nonetheless, for certain problems, it has been found that these adverse effects can be mitigated, leading to better outcomes. Specifically, it has been observed that if the method's exploration of the parameter space commences near a relatively stable model configuration, the method's performance may improve. Consequently, a strategy was devised to capitalize on the potential of this new training approach, which involves pre-training the model using a different supervised method before applying it to the desired task. We test this strategy on task involving partial data and find that it yields better results compared to pure self-supervised pre-training. Finally, we examine the method's reliance on its initial conditions and find that, in some instances, its performance improves when the model is trained for a shorter period. We speculate that this occurs because the method involves noise reduction, where the model learns to eliminate unnecessary parameters, leading to improved accuracy. Overall, our findings demonstrate that this innovative training method can enhance neural network training, and it offers promising possibilities for tackling complex tasks in computer science. Specifically, it may be useful in solving partial data problems, distilling complex models, and generating more accurate and stable training and inference processes. Future research will investigate the method's potential application in more challenging tasks. Additionally, it is planned that the method will be made accessible as an open-source tool

uncertainty in modeling potential energy surfaces for molecular systems is related to the "electronegativity volume effect."  This effect influences the energy by approximately 5-10 times the Hartree, and is dependent on the local electron density and the specific atoms present in a given molecule.  In order to better understand this effect, we created a family of potentials that incorporates its influence, using data from high-level quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) calculations on homonuclear diatomic molecules as a reference point.  Our results indicate that incorporating the electronegativity volume effect improves the accuracy of potential energy surfaces for molecular systems, and also mitigates a related issue where energies from perturbative methods are negatively biased.  Additionally, we found that incorporating the effect speeds up convergence towards the full many-body energy using perturbation theory, and also improves the accuracy of energy estimates derived from density functional approximations.  Therefore, we suggest that a model incorporating the electronegativity volume effect could be used to inform the construction of revised energy functional from high-level data, potentially leading to better performance in valence region energy matching and related tasks.  Finally, we demonstrate that our model can be adapted to analyze properties influenced by the electronegativity volume effect, such as atomic dipole polarizabilities.  Our research provides a framework and understanding that could inform future developments in energy functional construction, and also highlights the importance of valence region energy matching, since this effect influences energy differences that are typically on the order of a few Hartree.  Our method for characterizing the electronegativity volume effect could also be applied to the study of larger clusters of atoms, and can be used in analyses that rely on density differences, such as atomic radii computations.  Our model, and the related methodology for computing potential energy surfaces, have been made publicly available through open-source software available online. Researchers are particularly eager to develop indicators that can pinpoint the intensity and direction of societal preferences towards specific events or income redistributive situations. In this paper, we propose a new approach, based on a discrete choice model of voters' decisions, that yields a precise mathematical formula for an agenda's utility value - a measure of how happy or unhappy the electorate becomes as a result of choosing a particular option. By analyzing the electoral system's underlying structure, we are able to derive a clear expression for what we call 'electoral intensity' - a long-sought single number that indicates the magnitude and direction of societal preferences towards a given issue or income distribution scenario. Our results show that this intensity is equivalent to the average difference in voters' preferences, and that it applies universally to all types of symmetric voting systems. Consequently, we are able to test and confirm the idea that electoral intensity is an important factor in the success of left-wing revolutions, and to demonstrate the distinct differences in societal intensity across various political revolutions, whether related to income or not. Furthermore, our research reveals that electoral intensity is influenced by key factors such as the level of income inequality in society and the availability of alternative voting systems. Lastly, we offer a practical solution for estimating the electoral intensity parameter in real-world scenarios, thus making it possible to use discrete choice data from actual elections to calibrate and refine the model. Ultimately, our empirical findings provide substantial support for the notion that societal value systems can be effectively represented by a single, comprehensive measure - a long-held quest of economists and sociologists. 

  The paper concludes by outlining the theoretical and practical implications of our research, which spans three interconnected areas. Firstly, it examines the underlying logic of our model and its broader theoretical ramifications. Secondly, it explores the feasibility of estimating the electoral intensity parameter using data from past elections. Thirdly, it highlights the significant policy implications resulting from our discovery that the societal value system can be efficiently represented by a single, comprehensive measure - a threshold that many forms of group decision making, including corporations and governments, can also strive to achieve.

Nonetheless, existing approaches rely on visible profile components such as images, posts, and friend lists for similarity analysis. To date, no research has explored the use of account similarity networks based on hidden profile features.

  This study proposes a novel method for detecting fake accounts that takes into account both visible and hidden profile characteristics. To achieve this, we created a large dataset of Twitter accounts featuring 10 million randomly selected genuine profiles and 5 million fake profiles identified through Twitter's API. Subsequently, we employed network-based techniques to evaluate both visible and hidden profile features and compared the performance of six different clustering algorithms. Notably, our results indicate that account similarity networks based on visible features offer superior performance to existing detection methods, while incorporating hidden features enhances the accuracy of detection. Ultimately, a hybrid approach combining both visible and hidden features proved most effective in identifying fake accounts. Our findings offer valuable insights to social media platforms on enhancing their existing account detection methods. The proposed methodology and related data are available for public access at https://github.com/nikhilsoni/Twitter_Account_Clustering.

To aid in this process, a system called location planning has been developed with the goal of optimizing infrastructure placement by accurately forecasting demand at potential sites based on existing and projected customers. To meet this aim, a probabilistic model incorporating spatial dependence in demand has been created using the Bayesian hierarchical method. An approach to refine the model with historical data through Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulation has also been proposed. Furthermore, a simulation-based location planning method utilizing the Monte Carlo method has been proposed to choose the optimal sites. Finally, a simulation model has been proposed that combines these two approaches to determine the optimal location planning strategy when spatial correlation and historical data are considered. To validate these methods, a practical case study with an Italian telecommunications company has been employed. To begin, the company's current infrastructure and projected development were analyzed, resulting in a shortlist of potential construction sites. To optimize location planning, the model's parameters were estimated using the Gibbs sampling method, and the Markov Chain Monte Carlo method was employed to simulate the model. Subsequently, the Monte Carlo method was used to simulate the location planning model. Finally, a simulation model was proposed that integrates these two approaches to determine the optimal location planning strategy, which was found to align with the initially selected sites. The model's accuracy was evaluated using the mean squared error metric, with the findings indicating effective estimation of the mean and variance of the potential sites. Ultimately, the model's simulation led to a 6% reduction in construction costs for the Italian telecommunications company. This indicates the superiority of the spatial model over a basic model in predicting demand at a single site. Furthermore, the approach proposed for combining the model with historical data has been determined to be beneficial, resulting in a 3% reduction in construction costs in scenarios where the approach was applied. Finally, the model's accuracy in predicting the mean and variance of the potential sites was found to be superior to a basic model in sites with low correlation and better in sites with high correlation, resulting in a small error. The findings of this research show that the proposed methods can be utilized to determine optimal location planning strategies, considering both spatial correlation and historical data. This method permits the computation of the free Lie algebra's dimensions, thus providing a method to calculate the number of distinct systems of linear equations within a given free Lie algebra. This method has further implications in the context of physical applications, particularly in the field of Poisson brackets where exact solutions are highly desirable.  Ultimately, this algorithm may contribute to developing new methods in the field of control theory, where exact solutions can facilitate improved performance and stability. By formulating the problem as a marker-based place recognition problem, a novel marker placement algorithm is proposed to optimize sampling without a pre-defined map. Additionally, a recursive peeling method is introduced to construct a map from sparse fingerprint data. This method makes minimal adjustments to the robot's configuration at a time, ensuring stable and streamlined navigation through the environment, and thereby enabling more efficient data collection and mapping processes, especially in unfamiliar environments. Experimental results validate the effectiveness of the proposed methods by comparing them with existing approaches on real-world datasets. Moreover, a publicly accessible implementation of this technology is provided on GitHub. This architecture can be applied to various robot platforms using the same interface. Furthermore, the generated data can be accessed through the WiFi Map API, which supports mapping and localisation services in a wide range of domains. By leveraging this architecture, more efficient WiFi mapping and localisation can be achieved with improved scalability and flexibility. Overall, the proposed methods contribute significantly to the stable and efficient operation of WiFi-based mapping and localisation robots. \\

  This paper introduces an innovative method called Contrastive Domain Attention Network (CDAE) for combining thermal and visible face recognition. To minimize domain disparities, CDAE employs a contrastive loss to learn from paired images. To enhance cross-domain ear information extraction, CDAE incorporates Attention Mechanism in the learning process. In order to test CDAE's performance, a dataset consisting of 9625 paired ear images was created using an intuitive method. This approach surpasses the competition in the direction of thermal to visible face recognition, with a 4.64% improvement in accuracy. Furthermore, CDAE achieves superior performance on unpaired images, resulting in a 2.95% improvement in accuracy. Our experiments show CDAE's capability to operate in real-world conditions with an efficient time complexity. To date, CDAE remains the top performing method, surpassing the competition by a significant margin, with a particularly large advantage in the direction of thermal to visible face recognition. 

  The key techniques that contribute to the success of CDAE are its ability to operate in real-world conditions and minimize domain disparities. This approach shows promise in being generalizable and effective in other domains. 

  To test CDAE's cross-domain generalization, a method of constructing the paired ear dataset was designed. This method shows that CDAE can successfully learn from the data and perform well on test images. Their orphans' future relies heavily on international charity, highlighting the urgency of providing them with safe environments and emotional support. However, little research exists on children's experiences during and immediately after acute crises. To bridge this gap, our study focuses on children who have lost family members in conflicts, with the goal of uncovering the intricate and often overlooked aspects of their worldviews that may influence their well-being and resilience. To this end, we propose a novel and comprehensive framework called Children's Crisis Storyline Analysis Model (CCSAM), designed to uncover the depth and complexity of children's experiences. CCASM is a semiautomatic system that incorporates a mix of machine learning and human evaluation to classify children's crisis stories into coherent and coherent narrative sections, as well as identify key concepts and relationships within those narratives. Extensive experiments were conducted to verify CCASM's effectiveness, involving a dataset of 81K crisis stories collected through an online platform. Our analysis reveals CCASM's results to be 82% accurate, outperforming traditional machine learning methods. Furthermore, qualitative evaluations confirm that CCASM enhances human understanding of children's crisis experiences by capturing the depth and complexity of their stories. Ultimately, CCASM is expected to contribute to the development of more effective emergency response and long-term support strategies for children facing crises. Using numerical simulations of a modified version of the two-dimensional Navier--Stokes equations with randomly distributed external forcing and no spatial reflection symmetry, we investigate the development of local differences in heat transport.  These simulations show that, given sufficient time, the system consistently generates areas of heat transport anomalies where the temperature gradient's direction changes abruptly, accompanied by circulation patterns at the boundary.  Observations indicate that the time it takes for these anomalies to develop and the area they occupy follow an exponential distribution, suggesting that the generation of these anomalies is a periodic event.  Furthermore, when we increase the scale of these anomalies by changing the system's parameters in a way that affects the dissipation but not the overall structure, the time it takes for them to develop changes accordingly.  Interestingly, the effect of changing the dissipation level on this time is found to be independent of the spatial dissipation mode and the resulting heat transport anomaly's characteristics; hence, this time is predicted by a theory to take a specific value for an infinitely dissipative system.  Finally, we explore the possibility of applying our findings directly to the actual climate system by comparing the time it takes for large-scale heat transport anomalies to develop in our simulations with the time scales observed in climate data.  However, given the significant differences between our simulations and the climate system, including the presence of stable circulation patterns, known as stationary waves, which influence the heat transport anomaly's development, we conclude that the climate system's behavior from one year to the next is unlikely to be similarly consistent.  Nonetheless, the idea of there being a time scale on which the heat flux's direction changes significantly, and the associated physical process known as "heat cascade," is suggested to potentially be relevant to longer climate time scales, such as decades or centuries, and could, therefore, have implications for the study of long-term climate variability and change.  Consequently, we propose the formation of local and global heat transport anomalies as a new paradigm for understanding and studying the atmosphere and ocean's behavior on various spatial and temporal scales.  This point is particularly emphasized, as it could also imply that such scales of heat transport anomalies could be an essential factor in the coupling between the atmosphere and the ocean.  Ultimately, we emphasize the need for further investigation into the dynamics of local and global heat transport anomalies, and their role in the interaction between the atmosphere and the ocean, through observational studies and models that simulate the long-term climate system behavior. clever algorithm seeks the input of a human expert, and the primary challenge lies in accurately gauging the value of non-expert, automated data labels. As active learning methods increasingly rely on non-expertine labels, determining label quality becomes a top priority. Current techniques that assess label quality are, however, restricted to tasks with clear label flaws that can be identified by evaluation metrics, and they fail to account for instances where the similarity between data points hinges on random variables. To address this, we introduce two concepts that an optimal active learner can utilize to assess the quality of non-expertine labels: data similarity variability and label noise uncertainty. Data similarity variability measures the range of similarities between data points within a partition, while label noise uncertainty represents the likelihood that a label within a partition is incorrect. We develop two protocols for evaluating the quality of non-expertine labels on unlabeled data, and we demonstrate the effectiveness of these protocols in two scenarios, including one in which we simulate the ejection of a data cluster's labels and another in which we model the mixing of two distinct data clusters with noisy labels. Overall, our study illustrates the significance of assessing label quality and provides two specific methods of doing so, and we hopes that these contributions will pave the way for the further development of label quality assessment techniques in the future. (LISA) is poised to uncover a variety of mysterious astrophysical phenomena through measurements of gravitational waves, particularly at low frequencies. One potential LISA discovery is a new source of signal, which could originate from peculiar astronomical occurrences such as colliding neutron stars or black holes or alternative explanations like variations in the gravitational wave speed or gravitational reformulation of the scalar-tensor theory. As LISA approaches its operational launch date, the possibility of co-observing the predicted signal with other space and ground-based gravitational wave detectors needs to be considered. Since this prediction is based on frequent binary mergers, the frequency of these occurrences could make them distinguishable from other unknown LISA sources. To confirm this, we will examine the probability of simultaneously detecting these signals with ASTRACE, LISA, and ground-based detectors like LIGO and Virgo during the initial LISA operational phase. Specifically, we will calculate the total observation time and compare it with the total number of predicted mergers under the assumption that these binaries occur randomly. To validate this approach, we will verify that it yields consistent results for a real-time LIGO-Virgo O3 observation period. Ultimately, we found that there's a relatively high chance (~35\%) that LISA will begin operation alongside ($10^3-10^4$ Hz) or shortly after a ground-based detector detects a binary merger, which could significantly improve the likelihood of observing the predicted signal during the initial LISA phase due to the frequency of these occurrences. However, we found that the probability of observing the predicted signal during the initial LISA phase is relatively low (~4\%), which prompted us to explore two alternative scenarios. In the first scenario, we assumed that the predicted signal would exhibit a distinct feature, which would make it easily identifiable in the gravitational wave data. Under these conditions, we calculated that the probability of observing the predicted signal during the initial LISA phase would increase to around ~20\%. In the second scenario, we considered the possibility that the predicted signal could be indicative of a more complex astronomical occurrence, which would make it difficult to distinguish from other unknown LISA sources without more information. As such, we found that the probability of observing the predicted signal during the initial LISA phase in this scenario would be roughly ~5%. Ultimately, we concluded that while there's a relatively low chance of observing the predicted signal directly, there's a higher probability that LISA will begin or soon begin operation alongside ground-based detectors and, as such, may uncover the predicted signal through the analysis

Our approach allows for discrete-to-discrete, discrete-to-continuous, and continuous-to-continuous comparisons.  It adapts to support-turned-measure distributions and works effectively with finite, bounded domains.  Furthermore, this method produces accurate results for narrow convolutions of probability distributions, enabling the calculation of stable convolutional densities in the Bernoulli distribution family.  Implementation in a Python program is demonstrated below.

import numpy as np

def wasserstein(p, q, dim):
    # Compute the 1-D Wasserstein distance between two probability distributions
    return wass_for_1d_prob(p, q, dim)

def wass_for_1d_prob(p, q, dim):
    # Compute the 1-D Wasserstein distance between two probability distributions p and q
    L = np.array([[[1 / (k + 1) ** 2 for k in range(1, 101)] for j in range(dim)] for k in range(1, 101)])
    k_values, j_values, l_values = np.mgrid[1:101, 1:101, 1:101]
    potential_matrix = np.exp(L)
    k_div_j = np.divide(k_values, j_values)
    l_div_j = np.divide(l_values, j_values)
    log_p_potential = np.log(p) * potential_matrix
    log_q_potential = np.log(q) * potential_matrix
    sum_log_p_potential = np.sum(np.exp(log_p_potential), axis=2)
    sum_log_q_potential = np.sum(np.exp(log_q_potential), axis=2)
    wass_dist = np.abs(np.divide(1, 3) * (sum_log_p_potential - 2 * sum_log_q_potential + sum_log_q_potential.T))
    wass_dist_min = np.min(wass_dist)
    return wass_dist_min

Despite significant advancements in artificial intelligence, animals' ability to recognize objects remains a key biological capability that non-biological systems struggle to mimic.  A novel biological inspiration for object recognition presented in this paper reveals the importance of dust-covered sensory organs on locusts' ability to identify objects through touch.  It is demonstrated that the locusts use spatial and temporal touch patterns on its sensitive palps to differentiate between various objects, and this capability is further enhanced by the locusts' ability to apply varying amounts of force and duration.  A study on a versatile tactile system in animals for object recognition uncovers a more comprehensive and adaptable sensing system than existing artificial equivalents.  This research offers a new understanding of biological object recognition and provides an innovative method for developing more sophisticated artificial touch systems that can recognize objects.  Moreover, the potential of this system in developing advanced artificial limbs capable of object recognition is explored.  A key outcome of this research is the development of a Tactile Pattern Mode Decoupling network, a cutting-edge method based on a neural architecture that mimics the complexity of this sensing system, and it outperforms existing artificial touch systems in object recognition capabilities.  A simulation of this sensing system is performed on a synthetic touch data set that was created randomly, and a successful application of this sensing system on identifying objects in a robotics context is also presented.  A video showcasing the methods used in this research and their outcomes is available at https://youtu.be/-KQ03KTgB7c.  This work is a pioneering study in the field of touch-based sensing and recognition, and it marks an important milestone in bioinspiration, and it makes the accompanying code and data available at https://github.com/locus-sensing.  An article based on this research is published in Nature Machine Intelligence in December 2021.  An English version of this master's thesis is presented here.  It is an expanded version of the article and includes more detailed information on the research, and it is supplemented with additional figures and results.  A German version of this master's thesis is available at https://pub.hsr.harvard.edu/2022/01/69/.  An abstract of this master's thesis is presented below.  This master's thesis discusses a newly developed tactile sensing and recognition system that mimics the functionality of the locust's sensitive palps.  It is an advanced touch-based sensing system that outperforms existing artificial touch systems in object recognition capabilities.

Through the application of a external electric and magnetic fields, the grapheme's electrical properties undergo significant changes, ultimately resulting in a modified band structure. With considerations regarding transport physics, the influence of these fields on the electronic properties has been extensively studied. However, research examining the effects of trigonal warping on the graphene's electrical properties has been largely an area of unsatisfaction in the existing literature. In an effort to fill this knowledge gap, a thorough examination of the effects of trigonal warping on the graphene's electrical properties is presented, with calculations indicating that this phenomenon leads to the intensification of the elliptical flow in graphene. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the intensification of the elliptical flow results in an increased third harmonic generation in graphene. The influence of warping on the graphene's electrical properties has been fully incorporated in the calculations, resulting in a revised and invariable band structure for graphene, irrespective of the applied electric and magnetic fields. The revised band structure serves as the foundation for the computational model used to determine the nonlinear optical properties of graphene. The model, developed through the systematic examination of the effects of trigonal warping on the graphene's electrical properties, is grounded in the principles of transport physics, provides comprehensive information about the intensification of the elliptical flow and the nonlinear optical properties, and is applicable across the entire wave vector space. Moreover, it is found that the spatial distribution of the elliptical flow can be utilized to generate nonlinear optical properties at any point in the wave vector space. Current neuroimaging research relies heavily on diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) to gather data on white matter tract connectivity, yet its slow data collection speed limits analysis to a relatively small number of samples. Recently, a high-speed dMRI sequence called Axisymmetric Diffusion Imaging (ADI) was introduced, enabling the collection of a full-time frame of data in a single scan. Our research involved speed-optimized adi measurements using a 3T MRI scanner and a specialized array of 32 coils to gather data on 14 healthy subjects with 160 ms time resolution, 160 times faster than before. Our results compared adi data to those obtained with the more conventional Ball Stick Model, and further investigated spatial sampling and representation issues in adi data. Our findings were further confirmed through a study involving 40 new subjects who underwent either adi or conventional sequencing in alternating scans. Our research showed that faster sequencing in adi does not compromise its quality compared to the Ball Stick Model, and more importantly, revealed the benefits of higher spatial resolution in adi data without increasing data collection time, an important breakthrough in dMRI research. Our work offers various possible applications and future directions for research in fast dMRI.

A comprehensive literature review suggested that the Z boson could decay into three neutral particles, including a Higgs boson and a pair of neutral mesons.  Specifically, this search focuses on a scenario in which the Z boson decays into a hh and J/psi gamma transitions are excluded.  A data set containing 5.4 fb^-1 of proton-proton collisions, collected at 13 TeV, was used for the analysis.  A search for a Z boson decay into a hh with one photon emission has a mass sensitivity of approximately 35 GeV/c^2 for 5.4 fb^-1 of data at 13 TeV.  A scenario in which the Z boson decays into a pair of neutral mesons, with one meson decaying into a rhos and a photon, has a detected mass at 83.2 GeV/c^2 with a 95% confidence level. Consequently, this search provided limits on the cross-sections of two possible Z boson decays into a pair of neutral particles, namely into a hh and a pair of neutral mesons. Despite the potential, aluminium-ion batteries face significant challenges in achieving fast and long-lasting aluminium-ion insertion in various organic molecules. To overcome this issue, we developed a novel design of cross-linked polyaniline nano-fibers, allowing for high-speed aluminium-ion insertion with low degradation. With an ultra-fast insertion rate of up to 100 mC/s, our organic molecule-based 3D electrodes exhibit exceptional performance, including high capacities (300 mC/g at 100 mC/s, 150 mC/g at 1000 mC/s) and long lifetimes (up to 1000 cycles). Advanced characterization techniques have shown that the stability of the nano-fiber structure contributes to its remarkable aluminium-ion insertion properties, paving the way for efficient and scalable aluminium-ion battery production. Furthermore, our findings provide valuable insights for developing other stable and high-performance aluminium-ion batteries.  The unique design of our aluminium-ion battery, coupled with its attractive characteristics, holds great promise for fast and safe aluminium-ion insertion, which can be applied to a range of other organic molecules. By utilising advanced computational methods, we identified two key aluminium-ion interaction sites within the polyaniline structure and confirmed the findings through X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, demonstrating the potential of this design in achieving fast and long-lasting aluminium-ion insertion.  With the rise of aluminium-ion batteries, we are seeing a shift from traditional lithium-ion cells and a growing interest in using these cells for energy storage in the internet of vehicles (IoV). However, standard ion batteries fail to meet the high-speed charging and discharging requirements of IoV applications, exceeding 1000 mC/s in some cases. Our high-performance aluminium-ion cells successfully meet these high-speed needs, offering up to 1000 times faster operation than current ion batteries, and combined with our innovative charging techniques, make them an ideal choice for IoV applications.  The integration of our aluminium-ion battery in IoV has brought about a vehicle network where data is directly accessed (IoD), and vehicle data management is enhanced (IoMT). in semiconductor materials under photoexcitation are key phenomena studied in ultrafast materials research.  Excitons in direct bandgap semiconductors cannot form as they lack Coulomb attraction.  Tindall and colleagues in a 2018 study of photoexcited graphene discovered an analogous system in which electron-hole pairs gave the appearance of forming excitons.  This occurred because the pseudomagnetic field caused by the excitations led to mass asymmetry between the electron and hole mass equivalents.  A subsequent work by the same authors refined their model incorporating the effects of a real magnetic field. 

  Our research further investigates the influence of a real magnetic field on the asymptotic mass ratio.  It reveals that the mass asymmetry is insensitive to the field strength when the electron and hole masses have a mass-energy ratio greater than one, regardless of the strength of the pseudomagnetic field.  This occurs because the carrollian curvature causes a shift in the mass mass that is proportional to the inverse quark mass.  As a real magnetic field causes opposite mass shifts for electrons and holes, their ratio becomes insensitive to the field strength.  This leads to the formation of "massless" excitons when the ratio reaches a critical value.  Notably, this condition can be achieved with realistic levels of magnetic field strength in bilayer graphene. 

  The formation of "massless" excitons under real magnetic field conditions is comparable to a earlier model without a magnetic field, in which the ratio reached a critical value due to the effects of a pseudomagnetic field.  This demonstrates that two distinct mechanisms can lead to the formation of massless excitons in photoexcited graphene. 

  The discovery of "massless" excitons has implications for understanding asymptotic mass ratios in grapheme systems and reveals that the formation of massless excitons is robust against magnetic field strength.  It also opens up the possibility of observing these excitons through observation of infrared spectra in graphene systems. 

  The mechanism of massless exciton formation in graphene can be replicated in other systems in which the electron and hole masses are asymmetric.  This could involve asymmetric fermion systems in curvaceous and carrollian spaces, in both in and out of body effects.  This suggests that the formation of massless excitons is not unique to graphene but can also occur in other fermion systems under certain conditions. 

  The possibility of forming massless excitons in fermion systems where the electron and hole masses are asymmetric is confirmed.

We investigate the complexity of this model when the teacher's output is in a separate space and show that it requires at least $\Omega(nR)$ examples when the student's input has $n$ variables and $R$ is the range of the teacher's output. Recently, several approaches have been proposed to extract global features from CSI data using DNNs.  While these methods demonstrate superior performance and reduced feature dimensionality, they increase the number of trainable parameters and necessitate substantial training data.  To address these challenges and optimize feature extraction, this paper introduces a new approach using adaptive filters and sparse data representations for extracting global features from CSI data. Evaluations using a ray-tracing channel model in two different scenarios indicate the efficacy of the proposed approach, yielding a $5.2\%$ reduction in error performance at half the required training data and a $71\%$ reduction in trainable parameters with comparable error performance to a fully-parametric DNN. This issue is particularly pronounced in Indian languages which are often used in code-mixing form on various social media platforms.  For instance, Facebook data may contain Hindi words within English sentences or vice versa.  Consequently, there's a growing interest in developing models that can handle this type of language.  This research proposes a novel dataset consisting of nearly 50,000 sentences combining Hindi and English, alongside an accompanying model, MGLM-XLNet, which utilizes multi-language attention and contextual techniques to facilitate better language understanding.  Through comparative testing, it's shown that MGLM-XLNet surpasses current leading models in language processing capabilities.  This model's success relies on its ability to leverage key language elements including token representations, word and memory attentions, and a contextual technique called layer normalization.  This technique increases model accuracy by ensuring consistency in future predictions.  MGLM-XLNet's source code, data, and pre-trained models are freely available on GitHub.  This research also explores multiple training strategies, including the use of labeled data to improve model performance on code-mixing evaluation datasets.  Additionally, it's shown that fine-tuning MGLM-XLNet on labeled data enhances its performance on various evaluation metrics.  This research suggests multiple approaches for training models on labeled and unlabeled data, as well as performing hyperparameter tuning.  Finally, it's discovered that MGLM-XLNet performs better when trained on a combination of labeled and unlabeled data compared to models trained only on labeled data using all labeled data.  This effect is particularly pronounced on tasks where models are lacking in training data.  This research indicates the importance of combining labeled and unlabeled data to enhance model performance and adapt better to new linguistic combinations.  This research proposes several future avenues for research including exploring additional training strategies, improving model architecture, and enhancing transparency and overall understanding of model decision-making processes. This paper provides an in-depth examination of the previous studies on rigorously founding deep learning methods, with a specific focus on those based on graphical models, functional analysis and operator theory.  It also offers a new approach to applying the principle of maximum entropy, leading to the development of the entropy-regularization method and the establishment of a formal generalization bound.  This analysis demonstrates that maximizing the margin while minimizing the complexity of the model can effectively control overfitting and achieve better generalization results.  The proposed method is shown to be effective in various tasks such as semantic segmentation, object detection, and image classification, achieving comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods using empirical grid search.  This analysis reveals that a certain type of nonconvex optimization is inherently stable, and its application to deep learning can prevent overfitting without sacrificing marginal gains.  The foundations developed in this paper may lead to the creation of a 'theory machine' that can automatically design neural network architectures based on the requirements of a specific task.  This is a significant breakthrough in the application of theoretical results to practical problems in machine learning. SP) involves timing-based job-shop scheduling with dynamic processing times, subject to stochastic variability. This paper tackles the deterministic variant of DJSP, where processing times are predetermined, on shops with a single or multiple machines, operated by a single or multiple managers, under complete or limited information conditions. To address variations, managers utilize a shared risk-sharing rule, modulating machine usage by adjusting operation frequencies. Consequently, the problem reduces to a large convex optimization issue, solvable through the application of split-cohort age-of-relief sequencing (SARS) or optimal control techniques, for achieving efficient job scheduling and machine allocation. Experimental results indicate that SARS yields superior job sequencing outcomes compared to optimal control, particularly on smaller shops, while optimal control delivers improved machine allocation with significant job throughput enhancements. Furthermore, the risk-sharing policy effectively minimizes total variability, as evidenced by the observed reductions in expected variability and mean squared variability. Finally, the paper examines the computational requirements of finding optimal solutions, demonstrating that solving large problems becomes increasingly complex, both in terms of problem size and optimal solutions' distribution density. Ultimately, the findings highlight the challenges and possible methodologies for efficiently solving large DJSP instances. We also explore how the application of a dynamical nuclear symmetry energy, which varies with density, affects the $L$-parameter value, and show that such an effect increases the value of $L$ at high densities. Importantly, our study reveals that to determine the nuclear symmetry energy's slope parameter with sufficient precision, densities below about two thirds of the saturation density should be extensively explored. We also introduce a formula for calculating the slope parameter of nuclear symmetry energy, and evaluate the relative precision of this calculation compared to the precision derived from the QHGM's application to the simulated neutron-proton ratio. Our study further shows that the nuclear symmetry energy's value can be estimated by applying a dynamical nuclear symmetry energy formula, and that such an estimate agrees with the value obtained from the simulation of the neutron-proton ratio in the range of densities $0 \leq \delta \leq 2$. of computing $\varLambda_q(n)$, 
  which represents the highest non-negative integer that can be expressed as a linear combination of powers of $q$ with coefficients from the set of non-negative integers. 
  We also explore lower bounds for $\varLambda_q(n)$ in relation to $q^n$. 
  Specifically, we show that the ratio of $\varLambda_q(n)$ to $q^n$ is bounded by a polynomial in terms of $q$ and $n$. 
  This result holds for both prime and composite values of $q$, and it generalizes similar findings for binary linear codes with lengths up to $n$. 
  Furthermore, we provide estimates for the average value of $\varLambda_q(n)$, 
  particularly when $q$ is a prime number, by analyzing its proximity to $q^n$ and considering the logarithm of the number of possible combinations of powers of $q$ with non-negative integer coefficients. 
  These estimates confirm that the upper bound derived earlier is indeed tighter than the lower bound and that it approaches a specific constant value as $n$ becomes large. 
  Lastly, for prime $q$, we investigate the limit of the logarithm of $\varLambda_q(n)$ divided by $n$ and establish that it cannot exceed $\frac{\log q}{q-1}$. 
  This result holds for both prime and composite values of $q$. 
  Finally, when $q$ equals two, we verify that the least integer that cannot be expressed as a linear combination of powers of $q$ with coefficients from the set of non-negative integers is equal to $2^{2n}-1$. 
  This result is derived directly, and it leads to a simplified understanding of the related problem of computing $\varLambda_q(n)$ and enables the formulation of a more general problem in higher dimensions. 
  Finally, we propose testing the existing limits of which parts of this theoretical framework have already been explored and which areas require further investigation. 
  Overall, this article aims to create an accessible foundation for understanding the underlying mathematics of which integers can be expressed as linear combinations of powers of $q$ with non-negative integer coefficients, 
  and by doing so, it strives to promote further research in this field.

The study further reveals that a quantum computer can identify the critical threshold with a linear number of samples for any finite dimension $d$, which significantly improves the previous known result of $O(L^{d/2})$ samples.

  The second study focuses on discrete-time Markov chain (DTMC) on a lattice and shows that a quantum computer can exactly simulate DTMC for a linear number of steps, where the simulation is carried out with a linear number of samples. The study further demonstrates that a quantum computer can efficiently calculate the stationary distribution of DTMC on a lattice by performing a quantum walk for a linear number of steps. The research findings then apply these results to solve multi-kayle percolation on a lattice, which leads to new quantum algorithms for the model. Finally, the study reveals that a quantum computer can efficiently calculate the heat kernel of DTMC on a lattice for a linear number of steps, where the lattice can be of any finite dimension, which significantly improves the previous known result of $O(L^{d/3})$ for a three-dimensional lattice. The research findings from both studies are further discussed in terms of their potential applications and the current theoretical limits in the field.  The talk concludes by outlining future research directions based on the ongoing projects.  The quantum algorithms mentioned in the talk are also described in detail in arXiv papers 2206.09014 and 2206.09015. As oxygen binds to hemoglobin, the resulting changes in x-ray absorption coefficients create a distinguishable signal from the surrounding tissue. An alternative imaging method, transmission x-ray imaging, has been employed to capture differential images of oxygen saturation levels on a subject's finger. These images were then used to generate a 2D map of the spatial distribution of oxygen saturation. This methodology effectively measures changes in the x-ray transmission properties of the subject's tissue, accurately plotting a graph of oxygen saturation vs. time and confirming previous findings using radiographic imaging. Furthermore, an analytical model was developed to derive a precise mathematical equation for oxygen saturation as a function of depth, which was validated using data from the transmission x-ray imaging tests and found to accurately match measured values. Lastly, an approximation was made to determine the minimum amount of diffusion available to the tissue, which may be used in future research to estimate its effects on tissue damage. To address this challenge, we introduce a general approach for detecting and counteracting various backdoors present in a program's source code.  Our technique is versatile and enables the detection of multiple backdoors, including those with hidden functionalities, as well as the identification of a single type of backdoor.  By analyzing the dependencies of a backdoor-embedded program, we can pinpoint its presence in the source code and accurately detect different backdoors without causing interference from other types.  Furthermore, we enhance our method to detect backdoors in modified programs by tracking the changes in source code.  Comprehensive evaluations using 12,960 programs reveal that our approach achieves up to 99.8% success rate in detecting backdoors without interfering with other types, and up to 90.2% success rate in detecting a single type of backdoor.  Results also demonstrate that our method remains effective in cross-type attack scenarios, specifically when the attack and defense scenarios involve different types of backdoors.  To support the integration of our method in IDE tools, we develop an efficient and reliable implementation, which successfully detects backdoors in 99.6% of cases.  Furthermore, we verify the validity of our approach through theoretical analysis and 11,295 real-world tests.  Lastly, we highlight the potential for our method to be applied in various other systems, specifically smart systems.  To facilitate future research, we release our code and data, which can be accessed via this link: https://github.com/icalpine/Backdoor-Detection.  Additionally, we publish our research papers in two prestigious journals, including Journal of Information Security and Chinese Journal of Advanced Software Engineering.  Lastly, we present our findings at the prestigious Secure Software and Information Management conference.  This research is an extension of our initial research, which was published in an international conference. now well-characterized which in turn creates new opportunities for theoretical 
models. By extensively investigating HDMD properties, researchers can significantly 
expand the probing potential of future colliders. In this work, we thoroughly 
analyze various properties of HDMD found in recent studies. Utilizing the 
benchmark theoretical models, we examine two key characteristics: the interaction 
strength of HDMD particles and their mass relationships. Notably, we thoroughly 
evaluate the interplay between these properties and their implications for HDMD 
abundance at equilibrium, as well as their stability across a wide range of mass 
spectra within halos. In addition, we delve into certain non-equilibrium processes 
shaping HDMD dynamics, involving rapid non-relativistic and relativistic fragmentation 
events. Ultimately, our goal is to develop a comprehensive theoretical framework 
enabling theorists to develop theoretical models aligned with observed HDMD data. 
This alignment will enhance the effectiveness of future collider experiments in 
investigating theoretical models. Specifically, we anticipate that future HDMD 
data will enable the development of constraints on the interaction strength (f_N), 
mass relationships (m_i / m_j), and mass (m_i) of HDMD particles, as well as the 
mass and interaction strength of its antiparticle (anti-N). In particular, we find 
that future HDMD data will allow for more stringent bounds on the interaction strength 
of heavy particles (m_i > 100 GeV) compared to what is currently known. Similarly, 
our work reveals opportunities to improve constraints on the mass relationships 
(f_N * (m_i^2 - m_j^2)) in the high-mass range by up to an order of magnitude. 
This study also identifies key characteristics of HDMD found in its mass spectrum, 
including its width (Gamma_i), which has yet to be extensively investigated. By 
probing this width, future HDMD data will open doors to new physics domains, 
probing regions influenced by width and then decay time. Finally, our work 
investigates non-relativistic and relativistic fragmentation processes (p_i -> p_j + 
X), showcasing their significant impact on halo structure, particularly their 
fragments. Ultimately, our goal is to create a comprehensive theoretical framework 
for HDMD found in its halo. This framework will serve as a crucial guideline for 
next-generation collider experiments in investigating theoretical models,

In general relativity, the memory effect is characterized by an initial sudden strike and a prolonged gentle stroke. Previous research has focused on the strike memory in free fields, and this work aims to investigate the gentle stroke memory in free fields within the context of the relativistic quantum field theory. This gentle stroke memory is shown to be directly tied to the long-term behavior of massless free fields, and we explore this long-term behavior for both scalar and spin-1 vector fields. Furthermore, we evaluate the impact of radiation patterns in the context of spin-1 vector fields. Lastly, we provide a graphical representation of the gentle stroke memory for scalar and spin-1 fields, and outline future research areas, particularly exploring the possibility of establishing a connection between the gentle stroke memory and the strikememory in the context of interacting systems within the canonical and non-canonical frameworks for massless free fields.
